Summary of Child Node 1: Participants described the limited supply of electricity as the major challenge in coping with extreme heat, particularly among lower socio-economic populations. Frequent and prolonged power outages were commonly reported, occurring at various times of the day and night. Participants explained that electricity disruptions made indoor environments extremely uncomfortable and unbearable, especially in tin-shed dwellings where heat retention was perceived to be particularly high. Many participants stated that sleeping at night became difficult or nearly impossible during periods of load shedding due to the lack of fans and poor ventilation. Beyond such complaints, participants also highlighted the broader disruptions caused by power outages, including difficulties in accessing water, as electric pumps and water supply systems often became non-functional during load shedding. Inaccessibility to water also makes it challenging for the people to cope with the extreme heat. Some participants emphasized that, although heat itself could still be tolerated to some extent, the absence of electricity significantly intensified their suffering and was perceived as one of the most critical challenges during periods of extreme heat and heatwaves.

Summary of Child Node 1: Most of the participants described that during extreme heat, people sit outside their homes and spend time in open outdoor spaces as a common coping strategy. In informal settlements, many households reportedly have limited ventilation due to no windows, to which residents associated with concerns about theft and security. As a result, indoor environments often become excessively hot and poorly ventilated, particularly during electricity outages. To cope with these conditions, residents frequently rest in open areas with better air circulation, such as open spaces in front of their homes or nearby shops, open streets, railway tracks, and shaded areas under trees. Participants mentioned such spaces as comparatively cooler and more breathable, making them important and easily accessible means of coping with extreme heat.

Summary of Child Node 1: Participants described a range of adaptive strategies used to cope with extreme heat at both community and household levels. One KII participant referred to heat adaptation measures implemented in other countries, such as spraying water in crowded public spaces to reduce ambient temperature and adopting more flexible dress codes that encourage the use of lightweight and breathable clothing, including cotton half-sleeve shirts or t-shirts, even in formal settings. At the household level, lower-income populations reported using low-cost and easily accessible cooling techniques to reduce indoor heat. These included placing soaked cloths over windows to allow cooler air to circulate into the room, sprinkling water on floors to reduce indoor temperature, and pouring water on rooftops to cool the roof surface and minimize heat inside the home. Participants perceived these practices as practical coping mechanisms during periods of extreme heat and heatwaves.
